correspondence.finding: The southern and westward upper approach corresponds to the separately labeled Río Manso course and its junction with the receiving Sinú. The initial northern approach extends beyond the continuously readable Manso line on the inspected departmental map. Its channel identity is not established by a nearby label or by basin membership.

The receiving route turns north along the Sinú and passes through the mapped Urrá impoundment before continuing toward Tierralta. The pre-impoundment departmental map and later reservoir cartography distinguish this corridor from the western Río Verde and Esmeralda approaches.

The main corridor continues down the Sinú valley through the Montería, San Pelayo and Lorica settings to San Bernardo del Viento. Its coastal endpoint lies in the Tinajones delta setting west of Bahía de Cispatá. The generalized last cells do not establish a precise distributary, present shoreline intersection or surveyed mouth.

The initial Mexican portion follows a small headward corridor into the mapped El Coyote drainage in northern Altar municipality and runs north toward the international boundary. This is separate from El Plomo and the southward Río Sásabe/Altar receiving network. The first generalized cells are not assigned a precise tiny-fork name or formal source point.

After entering Arizona, the selected channel follows the repeatedly labeled Vamori Wash northwest, east of the Alvarez Mountains and south of the Sells/Artesa setting. San Luis Wash, Sells Wash, Baboquivari Wash and other tributaries are distinguishable separate approaches. The selection continues west to lower San Simon Wash and turns south; it does not include the full San Simon headwaters farther north.

The southward lower San Simon approach returns to Mexico. Its receiving Sonoyta corridor bends south in the northern Caborca projection before turning west and northwest around the border-range terrain. Caborca and General Plutarco Elías Calles cartography independently label this receiving course Sonoyta/Sonoita. The first model-fragment boundary is a subdivision of that course, not a demonstrated river-name transition.

The selection runs through the La Nariz/Valdez surroundings into the Sonoyta town corridor and continues northwest almost parallel to the international border. Its sequence of bends, neighboring ridges and town position match the mapped Sonoyta course; nearby Bajo San Francisquito, Burro Pardo and other desert channels are not substituted as whole-route names.

The western segment turns southwest and then south along the eastern side of the Pinacate terrain. It follows the mapped receiving corridor through the Cerro San Pedro/Sierra Blanca and Sierra San Francisco surroundings, passing the federal-road crossing and continuing down the coastal plain east of Puerto Peñasco. Palo Fierro and Guadalupe are distinguishable tributary approaches rather than synonyms for the selected whole route.

The lower state map directly labels A. Sonoyta and follows it to the coastal outlet plain near Playa Encanto, west of Estero Almejas. The selected coarse terminus belongs to this Gulf-margin setting east of Puerto Peñasco. It is not extended to a different estuary, a precise surveyed mouth or a present-day tidal inlet; minor shoreline/channel offset in generalized geometry is left explicit.

The short initial approach is on the northeast side of Lagunita Salada and joins the clearly labeled Arroyo Perdido valley to the west/south. The initial feeder is not separately named with confidence; no formal source point or complete Sierra de Blancuntre headwater is substituted for the selected start.

Repeated Arroyo Perdido labels match the long southward course west of Sierra Rosada, past El Escorial and along Valle General Racedo. The broad southern bend and succeeding east/northeast valley remain consistent with that mapped stream. The adjoining Zanjón Colorado and other side valleys are not whole-path names.

The northeast continuation passes below the separate El Mirasol/Arroyo Salado approach and proceeds on the mapped Perdido corridor toward Bajo de la Tierra Colorada. The source map distinguishes the northern Mirasol Chico/Telsen-side drainage and the southern Chubut-side country from the selection.

Near the western part of Bajo de la Tierra Colorada, the model turns east and then northeast beyond the explicitly drawn lower Arroyo Perdido course. A substantial terminal interval traverses the broad lowland and finishes at a northern wet/saline depression near the southern Telsen approach. The map does not show a continuous named Perdido channel along that whole modeled detour. Shared lowland location is not evidence for a present through-channel or a change to the Telsen name.

The research chapter describes Perdido as an ephemeral closed-basin drainage reaching Bajo de la Tierra Colorada, which also receives the separate Telsen system. This supports the regional receiving depression, not the identity or hydraulic continuity of every modeled terminal cell. No Atlantic outlet or present flow is asserted.

The first selected setting lies south of Eleodoro Lobos in mapped open agricultural/wooded country with contours and local tracks. The readable 1:100,000 first-setting detail does not establish a named source stream there. The selected southeast route toward Nueva Escocia is spatially separate from the prominently drawn Quinto corridor northeast of Fraga. No formal Río Quinto source or named upper tributary is assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: Nueva Escocia, Lavaysse and southern Villa Mercedes country
correspondence.finding: The selected upper-middle path traverses dune/contour and farmland terrain around Nueva Escocia and south of the Villa Mercedes–Lavaysse corridor. The map depicts separate small lagoons in the surrounding country, while Río Quinto runs through Villa Mercedes and Justo Daract farther north and northeast. No continuous mapped watercourse connects the full selected sequence through these plains, and the scattered lagoon names do not identify the whole route.

correspondence.component_scope: Southern San Luis to Villa Valeria–Del Campillo plains
correspondence.finding: Across the provincial transition and the middle reach, the selection continues southeast through predominantly farmland and dune/lowland mapping south of the Quinto. The named Quinto course through the Villa Sarmiento setting remains distinct to the north; it is not a selected receiving trunk. The route subsequently passes north and northeast of Villa Valeria toward the Del Campillo surroundings without a cartographically established continuous named stream.

correspondence.component_scope: Southern Córdoba lowlands and actual terminal setting
correspondence.finding: The lower selection enters a broad mosaic of marsh/depression symbols, scattered lakes, fields and low contours west and south of the Santa Magdalena/Jovita setting. Detailed original mapping covers its final southeastward continuation and places the endpoint in inland lowland country north-northeast of Pincén, close to the road and railway corridor. Neither a named river mouth nor an exact named terminal lake is established. The endpoint is not moved to a nearby lake label, to Bañados de la Amarga or to the Río Quinto.

The topographic evidence distinguishes the selected plains route from the neighboring named Quinto river and depicts multiple intervening terrestrial and low-depression settings. A whole-route natural-channel or receiving-system identity remains unsupported. A name-scope hold is appropriate; map omission alone does not prove permanent disconnection, absence of flood flow or absence of modern artificial drains.

scope_limit: MAIN_RIV groups and model mainstem roles do not establish a uniform name for every included reach, tributary or lake passage. Source observations support only the stated representative identity or hold.
publication_boundary: Own factual observations, attribution and official public URLs only; source originals, images, complete coordinates and private evidence remain omitted.
